name: PowerView - Get-DomainTrustMapping (Full Trust Map)
description: Enumerates ALL trust relationships across the entire AD environment — current domain AND every domain reachable through existing trusts. Unlike Get-ADTrust which shows only the current domain's trusts, Get-DomainTrustMapping recursively walks the trust graph to build a complete picture. Critical for identifying cross-domain and cross-forest attack paths.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY THIS OVER GET-ADTRUST ===
Get-ADTrust -Filter * → shows trusts FOR THE CURRENT DOMAIN ONLY
Get-DomainTrustMapping → follows each trust and enumerates trusts for each domain found

In a multi-domain forest, you might be in CHILD.CORP.LOCAL and not know that
CORP.LOCAL has a separate trust with PARTNER.COM. TrustMapping finds that.
Result: complete trust tree from any starting point.

=== READING TRUST MAP OUTPUT ===
  SourceName   → the domain this row's trust is configured in
  TargetName   → the other end of the trust
  TrustType    → FOREST (between forests), EXTERNAL (between domains, non-transitive)
  TrustDirection → INBOUND / OUTBOUND / BIDIRECTIONAL
  Transitive   → True = trust extends through the domain (forest trusts are transitive)

=== ATTACK PATHS BY TRUST TYPE ===
Parent-child (implicit bidirectional):
  → ExtraSids attack: compromise child → forge golden ticket with Enterprise Admin SID
  → Only works if SIDFiltering is not enforced (rarely is for parent-child)

Bidirectional Forest Trust:
  → Can Kerberoast users in the trusted forest
  → Can enumerate foreign group members
  → Cannot directly use ExtraSids (SIDFiltering usually enforced)

External Trust (domain-to-domain):
  → One-way or two-way
  → Less transitive, more restricted
  → Still can spray, enumerate users if bidirectional

=== QUICK REFERENCE ===
After running Get-DomainTrustMapping:
  1. Find any BIDIRECTIONAL trusts → those are pivot candidates
  2. Check for PARENT-CHILD relationships → ExtraSids if SIDFiltering=False
  3. List foreign domains → enumerate users there with Get-DomainUser -Domain <foreign>

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: In Active Directory the default security descriptor grants the built-in 'Authenticated Users' group read access to nearly every directory object (users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts) and their attributes. So any valid domain account — however low-privileged — can enumerate the whole directory over LDAP/SAMR without hitting access-denied, which is why this returns data without needing admin. Trust objects are readable; Get-DomainTrustMapping walks them recursively to draw the full inter-domain/forest trust graph.
defense.prerequisites: Valid domain credentials (any authenticated user) and network access to a DC (LDAP 389/636).
defense.impact: A trust map for lateral movement across domains.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1087.002] Broad/bulk LDAP queries to the DC (Event 4662 directory-service access; Microsoft Defender for Identity reconnaissance alerts); one host reading large swaths of the directory in a short window.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: Use built-in tools (net, AD module, dsquery) that blend with normal admin activity; throttle and scope collection; avoid the noisiest methods (full BloodHound sweeps, RID brute) where Defender for Identity is present.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects
